# Contracts: tenancy module
<!-- Generated by /speckit.plan Phase 1 -->
<!-- Reconciled with the shipped implementation 2026-08-26 (T072) -->

The public surface of `apps/web/lib/tenancy/`. Everything else in the codebase consumes
these; nothing else may reach Payload data operations
(`docs/tech-stack.md` § O risco nº 1 → nota Superado).

> **This file now describes what shipped, not what was planned.** Several names and
> signatures changed during implementation, always because something was measured. Each
> change carries its reason inline — a contract that quietly diverges from the code is worse
> than no contract, because it is believed.

## `getTenantScopedPayload(req, options?)`

```ts
type TenantScopedPayload = {
  find:     <T>(args: FindArgs)   => Promise<{ docs: T[]; totalDocs: number }>
  findByID: <T>(args: ByIDArgs)   => Promise<T | null>
  create:   <T>(args: CreateArgs) => Promise<T>
  update:   <T>(args: UpdateArgs) => Promise<T | null>
  delete:   <T>(args: ByIDArgs)   => Promise<T | null>
  tenantId: string           // resolved organization; throws before this if unresolved
}

getTenantScopedPayload(req: PayloadRequest, options?: {
  lookup?: HostLookup   // injected by tests — see Host resolution
  host?: string         // overrides host detection
}): Promise<TenantScopedPayload>
```

**Contract**

1. Every call runs with `overrideAccess: false` and the request's `user` — never Payload's
   permissive default.
2. `find`/`findByID` merge the caller's `where` with the tenant constraint as an **AND**;
   the caller cannot widen it.
3. `create` stamps `tenant`. `update`/`delete` take no `where`, so they verify by
   **constraining the operation itself**: the wrapper issues them with a tenant-scoped
   `where` on the id (`{ and: [{ id: { equals } }, byTenant(t)] }`) so a foreign document
   matches zero rows instead of being read then rejected — no read-modify race.
4. **[CF-8, shipped]** Clauses 2 and 3 apply **only to collections the scope registry marks
   `scoped`**. Stamping `tenant` on a global collection writes a column that does not exist;
   filtering by it returns zero rows forever. Neither failure announces itself, so
   `isScoped()` — not the caller, and not a hardcoded list — decides.
5. Unresolved tenant is an error (`TenantUnresolvedError`), never a silent "all tenants".

> **Cross-tenant reading is the plugin's job, not a flag on this client.** The plan proposed
> `allTenants: true` for masters. It was not built: spike S3 showed
> `@payloadcms/plugin-multi-tenant` composes access itself and adds **no** tenant constraint
> when `userHasAccessToAllTenants` returns true. A second mechanism for the same thing would
> be a second thing to get wrong.

### `getTenantScopedPayloadForRSC(options?)` — **[CF-4, added]**

An RSC has no `PayloadRequest` to pass, which the plan left unspecified. This is the
documented answer rather than something each page invents: it reads the forwarded host and
session from `next/headers`, authenticates through Payload, and returns the same client.

Callable only inside a Next request scope. Tests use `getTenantScopedPayload` with an
explicit `host` instead — which is why that escape hatch exists.

## Internal surface (the complete allowlist)

Everything that legitimately steps outside the request-scoped path lives here, inside
`lib/tenancy/`. This list is exhaustive by design — an earlier draft claimed "only two
bypasses" while the design already needed more.

```ts
// Explicit-tenant WRITE client, for operations with no request tenant (FR-032).
// The caller names the tenant; it can never be inferred from the host.
getSystemScopedPayload(tenantId: string, options?: { req?: PayloadRequest })
  : Promise<SystemScopedPayload>

type SystemScopedPayload = TenantScopedPayload & {
  // [CF-1] Declared here rather than discovered mid-implementation. Returns false when the
  // membership already existed — FR-021's no-op, reported so the caller can log the branch
  // without leaking it into a response.
  addMembership(userId: string | number, role: 'admin' | 'staff' | 'maker'): Promise<boolean>
}

// Reads that cannot themselves be tenant-filtered, because they exist to COMPARE tenants.
// Both return the narrowest possible value on purpose: anything richer would make them
// general-purpose unscoped readers.
unscopedLookupTenant(collection: string, id: string | number): Promise<string | null>
unscopedFindUserIdByEmail(email: string): Promise<string | number | null>
```

**`options.req` is not optional in practice.** A client built without it opens its **own
database connection**, so a hook writing a child row cannot see the parent row its own
operation just inserted. Measured: seed-on-create failed with
`Key (tenant_id)=(2) is not present in table "organizations"` until `req` was threaded
through. `docs/tech-stack.md` lists this as mandatory fix #1 for the XP ledger — it was
written down as a trap for feature 005 and walked into here first.

**Why a system client is unavoidable.** Seed-on-create runs when a *master* creates
organization B while served on some other host: a request-scoped client would resolve the
master's host and seed the wrong organization, or throw. The invite likewise writes
memberships into `users`, which org admins cannot see. Both need a tenant named by the
caller, not by the URL.

**Rules.** `getSystemScopedPayload` and `unscoped*` are never exported from
`lib/tenancy/index.ts`, are import-fenced from feature code by lint, and every consumer is
named in the plan. Each carries its own isolation test
(`tests/tenancy/system-payload.test.ts`, `tests/tenancy/unscoped.test.ts`), and the latter
asserts the module exports **exactly two** functions so a third bypass fails CI rather than
passing review.

## Host resolution

```ts
// The pure half — no next/cache, so it runs anywhere. This is what tests call.
lookupOrganizationByHost(host: string): Promise<{
  organization: ResolvedOrganization | null
  cacheable: boolean
}>

// The cached path production uses; the lookup is injectable.
resolveTenant(host: string, lookup?: HostLookup): Promise<ResolvedOrganization | null>
```

> **Split in two by spike S8.** The plan named a single `resolveTenantFromHost`. Measured:
> `unstable_cache`, `revalidateTag` and `headers()` all throw outside a Next request scope,
> so a resolver reaching for them on its main path could not be exercised by a test at all —
> SC-006 and CHK031 would have had nothing to run.

- `<slug>.<domain>` → the matching **active** organization (`status !== 'active'` resolves
  to `null`, including in the sovereign fallback).
- A host listed in `organizations.domains` → that organization.
- **Sovereign fallback:** when exactly one organization exists, any host resolves to it
  (`docs/tech-stack.md` § Modelo escolhido → Princípio central).
- Otherwise `null` → the caller returns 404 (never "first organization").
- The port is ignored when matching.

**`cacheable` is correctness, not performance.** Only a definite slug/domain match may be
cached. Under a single-organization install *any* host resolves via the fallback, so caching
`b.example.com → org A` would keep serving **org A's context on org B's subdomain** once org
B exists. `null` is equally uncacheable: a newly created organization would 404 until the
entry expired.

**The cache degrades, it does not gate.** Outside a Next request scope `unstable_cache`
throws, which would otherwise turn "no cache available" into "no tenant" — a 404 for a
request that should have resolved, in Payload's CLI, in tests, in any background job.
`resolveTenant` falls back to the uncached lookup.

**Semantics (one, not two):** resolution returns `ResolvedOrganization | null`. The choke
point turns `null` into a thrown `TenantUnresolvedError`; route handlers turn it into a 404.
Nothing swallows it silently.

## Same-tenant relationship validator

```ts
sameTenant(value: unknown, options: ValidateOptions): Promise<true | string>
```

Attached directly as a field `validate` on every relationship between scoped collections.
Rejects with a message naming **the field only** — naming the other organization would turn
any relationship input into an ID-ownership oracle, contradicting US8. Relationships to
global collections always pass.

**Two traps, both measured, both load-bearing:**

1. **Payload spreads the field config into the TOP LEVEL of the validate options**
   (`ValidateOptions = BaseValidateOptions & TFieldConfig`), so the target is
   `options.relationTo` — there is **no** `options.field`. Reading the wrong one made
   `normalizeRefs` return an empty list and the validator answer `true` to *everything*. The
   unit tests passed throughout, because they built the shape the implementation assumed.
2. **A partial update carries no `tenant`.** `payload.update({ data: { related } })` sends
   only the changed field, so the create-time null guard would wave every cross-tenant
   *update* through. The validator falls back to the stored tenant via `collectionSlug` +
   `id`, and treats a genuinely absent tenant as the create case — letting the tenant field
   own its own "required" error rather than competing for it.

## Scoped read endpoint — **[CF-9, added]**

```ts
scopedListEndpoint(collectionSlug: string): Omit<Endpoint, 'root'>   // GET <collection>/mine
```

Declared on every scoped collection. "Custom endpoints" is one of the four surfaces the
isolation harness must cover, and a surface with no subject tests nothing. A factory rather
than hand-written handlers: two copies drift, and the day one forgets the choke point is the
day the harness stops covering it.

## Invite

`POST /api/organizations/:id/invites` — org admin or master only.

```ts
canInvite(user, organizationId: string): boolean
resolveInvite(input: {
  organizationId: string; email: string; role: MembershipRole
  invitedBy: string | number; req?: PayloadRequest
}): Promise<'membership-added' | 'already-member' | 'pending-invite-created' | 'already-invited'>
```

**[CF-7] The orchestration lives here, not in the route.** It needs
`unscopedFindUserIdByEmail` and `getSystemScopedPayload`, both import-fenced — so writing it
in the route would have made the route trip the boundary it exists to respect, and the
tempting fix (an `eslint-disable`) would have put the two most dangerous functions in the
codebase into a file anyone can edit.

`InviteOutcome` is **never sent to the client**. It exists so the server can log which branch
it took while the response discloses nothing.

**Scope in this feature (FR-029).** There is **no e-mail transport** — the compose file ships
Postgres and MinIO only and no Payload email adapter is configured. So feature 000 ships
*membership resolution and the pending-invite record*; **delivery, token, expiry and the
accept/set-password flow belong to feature 004**.

| Case | Effect in feature 000 | Response |
|---|---|---|
| E-mail has no account | Creates a **`pendingInvites` row only** — no `users` record before the person accepts and agrees to the terms | `202 Accepted`, generic body |
| E-mail already has an account | **Adds a membership only** | `202 Accepted`, **byte-identical** body |
| Already a member | No-op | `202 Accepted`, identical body |
| Repeat invite to the same address | No-op | `202 Accepted`, identical body |
| Caller not admin of that organization | Nothing | `403`, resolved **before** the 202 |
| Malformed e-mail or body | Nothing | `400` — describes the request, not the directory |

The `202` responses must be indistinguishable — no account enumeration (US8, FR-021). Because
the branches do different amounts of work, the handler **responds first and performs the work
in `after()`**, so the reply carries no timing signal (SC-007). Verified over HTTP: three
branches, one distinct body by checksum.

**Idempotence is race-free by construction.** A repeat invite relies on the unique index on
`(tenant, email)` and insert-and-catch, not check-then-insert, which two concurrent requests
would both pass before either wrote. Note that Payload converts Postgres `23505` into a
`ValidationError` and **discards `code`**, so detection matches the composite index's field
names as well.
